title: Early arranging mistakes: writing too much
summary: Looking back on Glenn Miller days, he learned not to write everything and to think in colors and combinations; recalls hearing his first symphony.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: You mentioned your stint with Glenn Miller and you made your arranging mistakes then. What were the arranging mistakes that you learned about and didn’t do later?

Writing too much. Just writing everything. You know I’ll back up and say that the first symphony I heard was at Geneseo State Teacher’s College. My father and mother took us to see an orchestra, the Rochester Symphony. And I’d never heard anything like that in my life. And I hadn’t heard a real full big band at that point either, right? You know that was the first large ensemble live that I heard. You know in high school we had concert bands and all that. But anyway, when they took a break I looked at the stage and I could hear all of those instruments, just looking at the music stands. Now it sounds kind of stupid but when I first went on Buddy’s band and I would sit there and in the band itself that didn’t happen. But when I stood in front of a band, or sat in front of a band, and the band took a break, if I looked at the music stands I could hear all the music. Now I don’t need to look at the music stands, I found, with the Glenn Miller band, that you know I can hear the whole package. But the problem is is that you don’t have the experience of editing. I think maybe Bill Holman said it, you know, you write all your life and toward the end of your career you learn how to take stuff away, how to not put it down in the first place, how to not write. So I was writing too busily and too much stuff. And of course Buddy DeFranco would give me criticisms and comments like that because he worked with everybody. And a lot of it took hold. And then by studying the Glenn Miller scores, like Bill Finegan’s scores and stuff like that, I learned a lot. Space is very important.

Yes. If you look at a score and everybody’s playing all the time, you have trouble. But I know in the past I’ve had instances where I look at a score I’ve written and, especially if it’s for a large group, and, “Gee I haven’t written anything for the bassoon in 20 measures, I’d better give him something to do.” And that is not really the way to think I guess.

No. Not at all. You have to think in colors and combinations. You know with the jazz big band you think you’d run out of colors but you don’t. You can always find new combinations. You could never use up all the devices.
